machine.name: Desktop PC, 2025
machine.note: A micro ATX build with a liquid cooled processor. Nothing here is exotic; every part is something you could buy off a shelf this year.

parts.label: Side panel
body: For the first thirty years of the PC, the box was beige steel and the point was to never open it. Glass panels arrived once builders started treating the inside as something worth looking at, and once cooling shifted from one small fan to a managed flow of air through the whole case.

parts.label: Liquid cooler
parts.spec: 240 mm radiator, two 120 mm fans, pump on the processor
body: The original IBM PC processor needed no cooler at all. It produced roughly two watts of heat, about the same as a phone charger doing nothing, and the only fan in the machine was in the power supply.

This is a closed loop liquid cooler. The pump sits on the processor and moves fluid through the two tubes to the radiator at the side of the case, where the fans blow the heat out. Water carries heat far better than air, though a good air cooler still matches most of these, and this adds a pump that can fail.

parts.label: Processor
body: The processor carries out the instructions that make up every program running on the machine. This one contains billions of transistors, the microscopic switches that do the actual work, in a piece of silicon roughly the size of a postage stamp.

It has eight cores, meaning eight separate units that can each work on a different task at the same time. That matters more than it sounds: for about twenty years, chips got faster mostly by running the same single core at a higher speed, and then that approach hit a wall.

parts.label: Memory
parts.spec: 32 GB DDR5, 6000 MT/s, four slots filled
body: Memory, or RAM, holds whatever the machine is working on right now. It is fast and temporary; switch the power off and everything in it is gone.

There are 32 gigabytes here. The original IBM PC shipped with 16 kilobytes, which is roughly two millionths of this. What changed is not only the amount but what the amount is for, since a single browser tab today can use more memory than an entire computer had in 1995.

parts.label: Graphics card
body: The graphics card draws what appears on screen. It is the largest and usually the most expensive part in the machine, and it has its own processor, its own memory and its own cooling.

Early PCs had nothing like this. A display adapter in 1985 stored a grid of characters and colours and left every calculation to the main processor. The shift to a separate chip doing millions of parallel calculations is the reason a game today looks the way it does, and it is also why these cards now handle work that has nothing to do with graphics at all.

parts.label: Storage
body: Storage keeps files when the power is off. This drive is a stick of flash memory chips shorter than a finger, lying flat against the motherboard with no cable and no power lead of its own.

Its predecessors were mechanical: spinning metal platters with an arm that physically moved to find data, so the wait depended on where on the disk the data happened to be. Removing the moving parts made storage roughly two thousand times faster to respond, and that single change did more for how quick a computer feels than any processor upgrade of the same period.

parts.label: Power supply
body: Wall power arrives as alternating current at 120 or 230 volts. Every component in the machine needs direct current at 12, 5 or 3.3 volts, and this box does the conversion.

It is rated at 850 watts. A typical desktop in 1998 used a 200 watt supply and rarely drew half of it. Almost all of the growth since then sits in two components, the processor and the graphics card, and the machine is designed around getting power to them and heat away from them.

parts.label: Case fans
parts.spec: 2 x 120 mm on the radiator, PWM controlled
body: These two fans pull air through the radiator and out of the case, so they are cooling the processor rather than the case in general.

PWM stands for pulse width modulation, which is how the motherboard varies fan speed instead of running them flat out. It reads the processor temperature several times a second and adjusts, which is why a machine gets audibly louder partway into a game.

parts.label: Expansion slots
body: Four slots, and once the graphics card is in, three of them stay empty on almost every build. That is worth noticing, because a PC in 1996 had five or six and every one was likely to be full.

A machine of that era might carry separate cards for sound, for a modem, for video capture, for extra ports, and for a while a card that did nothing but calculate physics for games. Each was absorbed into the processor, the graphics card or the motherboard, and the slots emptied out.
parts.hint: Four slots. Once the graphics card is in, three of them stay empty on almost every build.

parts.label: Rear ports
parts.spec: Audio jacks, USB, Ethernet, video out
body: Three small jacks handle audio, and they cost the manufacturer almost nothing. For about fifteen years this was a job for a separate card that people saved up for, compared carefully and argued about.

The PC shipped with a speaker that could produce one square wave tone. Games worked around that limitation for years, then sound cards turned the PC into something you could listen to, and then the whole capability shrank into a chip on the board and stopped being a purchase decision.

parts.label: SATA ports
parts.hint: For drives that still need a cable. Most builds now leave all four empty, because the fast drive plugs flat onto the board instead.

parts.label: Power connectors
parts.hint: The 24-pin feeds the board. The separate 8-pin runs straight to the processor's voltage regulator, and it was added in 2000 because the Pentium 4 needed more current than one connector could safely carry.

parts.label: Network
parts.spec: 2.5 Gb Ethernet and Wi-Fi 7, both onboard
parts.hint: Both built in and effectively free. In 1988 a network card cost more than a hard disk and was something only offices bought.

parts.label: Motherboard
body: Everything plugs into this. The board carries power to each component and provides the wiring that lets them talk to each other, at speeds where the physical length of a copper trace starts to matter.

This one is micro ATX, a shorter version of the ATX standard that arrived in 1995 and dropped the lower expansion slots. The layout has barely changed in thirty years, which is why a case bought today fits a board designed to a much older specification. What has changed is what the board no longer needs to provide.
